messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mohammad is a 38-year-old Middle Eastern man who works as a hairdresser in a bustling salon. He recently sought help due to the debilitating effects of his PTSD symptoms stemming from a life-threatening illness he experienced several years ago. Mohammad was diagnosed with acute leukemia, and the harrowing experience has left lasting psychological scars. Mohammad’s traumatic memories often resurface through specific triggers that can disrupt his daily functioning. For instance, when he wakes up from nightmares about being in the hospital, the vivid images and sensations flood back instantly, causing a surge of fear and horror. These nightmares are particularly potent because they transport him back to the moment when doctors informed him about the severity of his condition and the dire implications it held. Even mundane activities can trigger intense reactions. For example, a routine medical examination brings on overwhelming physical reactivity; his heart races, and he feels an immediate sense of danger as if he were still in the hospital. The photos from that time—pictures of him hooked up to IVs or lying in a hospital bed—are especially distressing. Each visual cue sets off a cascade of negative emotions and bodily sensations. When Mohammad recalls these experiences, he often smells antiseptic and other medical odors associated with the hospital environment. These olfactory cues trigger both physical pain reminiscent of his ordeal and an intense emotional response without any clear image—just a visceral sense of anguish and helplessness. This combination makes him believe that his body is unreliable, constantly betraying him by reacting as if he were still in danger. Mohammad has come to view his body as the enemy, perpetually tense and on high alert. He feels this tension acutely during moments when he encounters medical-related triggers, which then intensify his negative emotions and physical reactivity. This cycle exacerbates his fear that he is losing control of himself and going crazy, leading him to avoid any situation reminiscent of his illness. His occupation as a hairdresser provides a daily backdrop for these experiences. The sterile smell in the salon sometimes reminds him of hospital environments, causing immediate anxiety and tension. He avoids clients who look ill or request treatments that remind him of medical procedures. This avoidance has strained his professional relationships, leading to fewer appointments and reduced income. The negative appraisals Mohammad holds about his body further reinforce his threat perception. When he feels the emotional intensity without a clear image, it convinces him that his reactions are irrational and a sign of instability. These beliefs then feed back into his triggers, making each encounter with them more fraught and distressing. Mohammad’s memory also plays a critical role in this cycle. When he smells antiseptics or feels pain in certain parts of his body, it reignites his sense of danger and negative emotions. The emotional intensity without clear images further intensifies the threat, making him feel as though he is reliving the trauma. These interconnected experiences have led Mohammad to a point where he recognizes that his life has become unmanageable due to his constant fear and distress. He hopes for relief from these overwhelming feelings and seeks therapy to regain control over his reactions and improve his quality of life. The most pressing concern for Mohammad is the fear that his symptoms will worsen, leading him deeper into a spiral of anxiety and avoidance.
